sam_choi: Quick thread—I'm chasing a tail-latency regression that seems correlated with KV cache misses. Did a short nsys run, attaching command and timeline snippet. Any obvious blind spots in my capture flags?

sam_choi: ```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --duration=20 --output=reg-kv-2026 
# ran against a load generator that toggles kv hit-rate to force evictions
```

maria_g: Good start. A few quick notes: 1) 20s can be noisy for sampling-based views—if you can afford it, extend to 60s for stable osrt stacks. 2) Use capture-range=nvtx:mark_start,mark_end in the harness so you only record the region where eviction happens (smaller files, clearer timeline). 3) If file size balloons, try toggling off osrt and rely on nvtx+cudatrace for kernel-level ordering.

alex_rm: Also check whether your load generator pins threads/processes. I saw misleading cpu sampling when the process migrated. If you can run with taskset or --capture-range=process:<pid> it helps align CPU stacks to the right process.

sam_choi: Noted. I did see one pattern in the timeline: after a KV miss, we get a small memcpy burst (~0.8ms) then a kernel called "attention_kv_update" which was ~2.3ms longer than usual and then a cascade of short kernels. Wondering if kernel selection (fused vs non-fused) flips when sequence length changes after eviction.

jen_perf: That matches a recent change: the kernel selector falls back to a generic concat path when cached KV layout isn't populated, so you get extra memcpy and a different launch config. If you can capture kernel names in the timeline, filter for the launch params—look for changes in grid/block or workspace allocation NVTXs.

maria_g: Yep. Add NVTX ranges around the KV write path: NVTX_PUSH("kv_write_start") / NVTX_POP(). Then in nsys you can filter by name and compare the CUDA API calls around that range. Also export to SQLite (--export=sqlite) for quick SQL queries on kernel durations across ranges.

sam_choi: Example capture command I'll try next (longer + focused):
```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,cublas,osrt --capture-range=nvtx:kv_write_start,kv_write_end --duration=60 -o reg-kv-focused --export=sqlite
```

alex_rm: One more: if you're trying to measure tail latencies, make sure to run at steady QPS long enough to collect many samples. Sampling-based stacks (osrt) are great for hotspots but you need sampling density. For deterministic traces, toggle sampling off and capture the exact API/kernels for a short sequence using nvtx boundaries.

jen_perf: When you do the long run, watch for intermittent kernel name switches. I usually grep the sqlite table: SELECT name, COUNT(*), AVG(duration) FROM cuda_kernels GROUP BY name ORDER BY AVG(duration) DESC; That quickly shows if a new kernel appears in the slow path.

sam_choi: Ran the focused capture. Quick findings: inside nvtx range I see attention_kv_update split into two launches for the miss case (first is small memcpy-ish, second is compute). The second launch has a different grid config (blockDim.x 128 -> 256). That change maps to 1.8–2.5ms extra per request under heavy load.

maria_g: Sounds like kernel selection logic triggers a different tiling when KV is populated vs cold. If you can, add a microbenchmark that exercises only the kernel selector path and dump selected kernel names/params to logs—easier to iterate than full nsys runs.

buildbot: [deploy-bot] Capture upload complete: s3://redwood-profiles/reg-kv-focused.nsys-rep (size 420MB), sqlite export at s3://redwood-profiles/reg-kv-focused.sqlite

sam_choi: Thanks all — next steps: 1) add NVTXs around selector and kv write 2) run longer focused capture with --export=sqlite 3) build tiny unit that repeatedly toggles cache to reproduce selector flip. Will post results. :thumbsup:
